video_title: Lawfare Daily: How Terrorist Groups are Using Artificial Intelligence
transcript: This is Daniel Bman. I'm the foreign policy editor of Lawfair and I'm here with Trisha Bacon, professor at American University and Antonia Julich, who is the international security lead at the Cambridge program on AI science and policy. We are here today to discuss artificial intelligence and how terrorist groups might use it and also its implications for counterterrorism. Um, and Antonio, I want to begin with you. Um, you just released a major report on how Boka Haram and Nigerian groups in general are using artificial intelligence. Uh, for our listeners who haven't read it, it's really fantastic. It's it's groundbreaking research. Um, and let me start by just asking you a few basic questions. Where and how are these groups using it? What problems are they having? Um, start with that, please. Yeah, thank you so much and thanks for having me. So what I found was that AI has become embedded really as a general purpose technology that can provide information across the full insertion cycle. So by that I mean um from assisting with how to prepare attacks to how to execute them to how to analyze failures afterwards and learn from them. Um yeah, one could really say uh it serves as a 24/7 operational assistant to Bookeram. And there were a couple of domains and specific examples that respondents have given me. Um one for example is getting weapons advice. So how as many of you know um a lot of these groups seized their weaponry, military equipment generally is by uh yeah seizing it from um from soldiers and by um raiding military bases. And so in the past whenever they uh got hold of weapons they were not familiar with they had to reach out to people in the network had to wait to hear back from ISIS and other operatives uh to receive online assistance or to wait for inerson trainers to come help them. Now the new rule is that whatever you get, you bring it back to the camp. Commanders uh type in the serial number um the model and this way they learn uh what type of weapons they have and how to service and troubleshoot. Um that of course um makes life much easier. There's less of a delay and just provides instant help. Um, another area is getting advice um on like tactical and uh strategic uh questions that they have and that ranges from brainstorming new ideas on how to respond to new counterterrorism measures to getting specific technical input on how to best implement tactics. Um they said, for example, that they learned how to carry out more effective and better coordinated attacks by deploying smaller units. And also one example that has gotten quite a bit of attention is that for example they learned how to jump over defensive trenches that the Nigerian military built around their own bases and towns with motorcycles and that was an obstacle in the past but then not anymore. Yeah. And one uh other area that I found quite concerning is that they uh get a lot of help with how to improve the design of their explosives. So that includes learning what additional chemicals uh to to include uh that make their own IEDs more powerful on how to diffuse unexloded bombs to extract the military grade explosive material and repurpose it in their own IEDs. Yeah, as one commander put it, trial and error can kill you. AI gives you accuracy. So it really helps them to bridge a lot of the technical gaps that they have encountered in the past. And yeah, what I found quite striking about these use cases was that while we were still discussing uh the risk of AI generated propaganda and misinformation, Bram already moved way past that and understood that AI can do so much more than that. >> Um so what your report makes very clear is the kind of wide um in very different ways that Boo Haram is using it. However, it's a big organization and you know I'm a professor at Georgetown University. I work at a think tank. I care at lawf fair.
